props.title: Seconds
props.initialSlug: Desperate man trades his life for sinister makeover

sections.content: John Frankenheimer's **Seconds** (1966) stands as one of the most unsettling psychological thrillers of the 1960s. Shot in disorienting angles by James Wong Howe, this paranoid nightmare follows a middle-aged banker who undergoes experimental plastic surgery to start a new life. The film's themes of identity crisis and corporate manipulation eerily predicted our modern obsession with reinvention and youth. Like **Invasion of the Body Snatchers** (1956) before it and **The Stepford Wives** (1975) after, Seconds taps into deep American anxieties about conformity and authenticity.

movies.slug: A surgeon attempts to reconstruct his daughter's disfigured face through questionable means

sections.content: The film's influence ripples through later works about identity transformation and corporate malaise. **Fight Club** (1999) echoes its themes of masculine crisis and rebirth, while **Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind** (2004) shares its questioning of memory and identity manipulation. Rock Hudson's against-type performance as Arthur Hamilton/Tony Wilson represents his most challenging role, deliberately subverting his romantic leading man image into something darker and more complex.

Frankenheimer's direction employs techniques that would later become hallmarks of psychological horror. The fish-eye lenses, Dutch angles, and extreme close-ups create a sense of claustrophobia that influenced films like **Rosemary's Baby** (1968) and **The Parallax View** (1974). The surgery sequences, shot in stark black and white, remain some of the most clinical and disturbing scenes in 1960s cinema. SUBHEAD: Corporate Horror and Identity Crisis

movies.title: The Game
movies.slug: A wealthy banker's life unravels when he participates in a mysterious game that blurs reality

sections.content: The film's exploration of corporate manipulation predates many similar narratives. Its shadowy "Company" that offers second chances anticipates the sinister organizations in films like **They Live** (1988) and **Dark City** (1998). The way it frames American success and reinvention as a form of horror speaks to contemporary films like **Sorry to Bother You** (2018) and **Get Out** (2017), where personal transformation comes at a devastating psychological cost.
